In brief

Parody. "O'Nolan, clad in shining armour [...] the winged speech of the seadivided Gael": when John Wyse Nolan enters the bar and the Citizen asks him, "What did those tinkers in the city hall" (the disesteemed councillors of the Corporation) "decide about the Irish language," mocking language once again skewers the Irish Literary Revival hope that Ireland can recover a lost medieval grandeur. The praises are overblown, and the suggestions of historical greatness are undercut by numerous ironies.

At more length

In yet another jab at the 19th century fashion of adding a noble medieval "O" to surnames—other parodies have created O'Bloom, O'Ryan, O'Bergan, O'Dignam, and O'Ciarnain—Joyce turns John Wyse Nolan into "O'Nolan." Like the dauntless O'Bloom, who was "bedight in sable armour," this knight is "clad in shining armour." He follows a lord, "the puissant and high and mighty chief of all Erin." Praising the Citizen as a kind of High King exaggerates to an absurd degree the deference which the other men in the bar accord him, and adopting medieval naming conventions does not turn barhounds into heroes.

The parody blends contemporary political reality with details from the past. O'Nolan reports that the Corporation met "in the tholsel." This ancient municipal center probably dates back to the 12th century, because records in 1311 refer to the "new" one in High Street. Through the centuries the Tholsel—a traditional name for administrative buildings in Irish cities—housed a guild hall, a jail, a courtroom, meeting spaces for the Mayor and Corporation, and even in the 1640s a Parliament House. The medieval building was demolished in 1676 and replaced with a grander structure, which in turn was demolished near the beginning of the 19th century. (Douglas Bennett gives a date of 1791, but it seems that at least some of the sprawling structure was not pulled down until about 1820.) In the 1850s the Dublin Corporation purchased the majestic building on Cork Hill that had formerly housed the Royal Exchange. Since then it has always been known as City Hall. Calling it the Tholsel indulges historical nostalgia.

O'Nolan calls the Corporation members "grave elders of the most obedient city, second of the realm." Dublin's motto, displayed on the city's coat of arms and inventively mangled many times in Finnegans Wake, is Obedientia Civium Urbis Felicitas ("the citizens' obedience [produces] the city's happiness"). Like the Tholsel, this emblem is old, but its historical context ironically undercuts the theme of Irish independence. It dates to the early 17th century when English rule of Ireland was being consolidated, so it would seem that Dubliners intended it to proclaim their loyalty to the crown—an inference that Joyce stresses by calling Dublin, an imperial capital from its earliest days, "the most obedient city."

Further ironies lurk in calling it "second of the realm." The boast that Dublin was the Second City of Great Britain dates to the glory days of the Georgian era. It became widespread in the 19th century and no doubt boosted civic pride, but at the cost of advertising Dublin's subordination to London, and by 1904 the claim had become tenuous: Belfast, an industrial powerhouse, was nearing Dublin in population and had probably surpassed it in wealth.

The city councillors begin with "due prayers to the gods who dwell in ether supernal," mapping Ireland's heroically polytheistic pagan past onto the humdrum contemporary business of invoking the Christian god. Then, in their "solemn counsel," the city's representative discuss whether "they might, if so be it might be," restore to honor the "winged speech of the seadivided Gael." The concluding epithet evokes millennia of Celtic migration. Seas separate the Irish from their Scottish, Welsh, and Cornish cousins and from the Bretons in northern France—and, as Gifford notes, all of these peoples were supposed to have come originally from northern Spain. It seems likely that the phrase also refers to the great diaspora prompted by the famine of the 1840s, in which millions of Irish people emigrated across the Atlantic Ocean.

Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner report that Fritz Senn has discovered the source of this phrase in a poem by Thomas D'Arcy McGee (1825-68), an Irish Catholic who participated in the Young Ireland uprising and then fled arrest to the United States in 1848, before moving to Canada in 1857 and becoming a leading parliamentary advocate of Canadian nationalism. In later life McGee opposed armed revolution and he was assassinated by a member of the Fenian Brotherhood from Montreal. "Salutation to the Celts" speaks of Celts in Ireland, Scotland, Iona, Wales, ancient Britain, northern Spain, Brittany, and North America, as well as Irish soldiers who serve the British empire in India. It praises the indomitable spirit of the Gaels but dwells on their long history of loss. Erin is "fallen," Scotland is "changed," the power of Mona is "small," Merlin's prophecies "degenerate to tales," and Iona's cloisters are "bemoan'd by northern gales." Each stanza concludes with the same stirring line. This is the first of four:

Hail to our Celtic brethren wherever they may be,
In the far woods of Oregon or o'er the Atlantic sea—
Whether they guard the banner of St. George in Indian vales,
Or spread beneath the nightless North experimental sails
One in name and in fame are the sea-divided Gaels.

The "seadivided Gael" concludes and epitomizes the parody's theme of heroic striving blasted by historical reality. Any decisions the councillors may make about reviving their people's "winged speech" will swim against powerful tides.

John Hunt 2026
